*Ag Secretary Rollins Says USDA Will Use New Tech to Improve Crop Production Estimates
Agriculture Department Will Use Satellites, Computer Models to Modernize U.S. Crop Data Reporting
The Agriculture Department is implementing changes to improve how it gathers and reports data on U.S. crop production.

The department plans to modernize how U.S. farmers report field data to the agency, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said Tuesday that in a speech at the Farm Progress Show in Boone, Ohio. It will also begin a pilot program to include tools like satellite imagery and computerized models to create more accurate forecasts of how many bushels of crops farmers grow across the country.

These and other measures are expected to improve the transparency of the data the USDA publishes, which have been questioned by farmers and analysts alike in the midst of downsizing and a move of agency headquarters to Kansas City last year.

"This plan brings USDA agencies together, breaks down outdated information silos, and applies modern technology to provide producers and rural communities with better service," Kip Tom, Special Advisor for Data Modernization, said in a statement.

As part of the effort to improve its estimates, the USDA said in a document detailing its modernization plans that it will collaborate more with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, NASA, to aid with "remote sensing, soil moisture, crop yield modeling, satellite mission planning, and joint research programs."
"This plan puts farmers first by cutting burdensome red tape, using modern tools, and ensuring producers have a stronger voice in how USDA collects and reports agricultural data," Rollins said.
The USDA's modernization plans are expected to boost the number off farmers who take part in the department's surveys.

"Farmers frequently get the mailed surveys late and they take a while to fill out," Ag Bull Trading analyst Jim Wiesemeyer said. "A push should and probably will be done to have farmers input survey responses on their computers and/or other devices."

The data collected informs the estimates that the USDA publishes in reports like its monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report, which is closely watched by grain futures traders. This month's report is scheduled to be published on Sept. 11.
